#10098. Designing the hf CLI as an agent-optimized way to work with the Hub

hf is the official command-line entrypoint to the Hugging Face Hub. Anything you can do on the Hub from the Python SDK, you can do from your terminal: download and upload models, datasets and Spaces; create and manage repos, branches, tags and pull requests; run Jobs on HF infrastructure; manage Buckets, Collections, webhooks and Inference Endpoints.

The hf CLI has been primarily built for our users over the years. But it's now increasingly used by coding agents: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and more. So we rebuilt it to make it work for both audiences at once. This blog post summarizes what we did, and how we benchmarked it. We found that on complex, multi-step tasks the no-CLI baseline (an agent hand-rolling curl or the Python SDK) uses up to 6× as many tokens as the hf CLI.

We started tracking agent usage of the Hub in April 2026. The hf CLI (and the huggingface_hub Python SDK it's built on) detects when a coding agent is driving it by reading the environment variables agents set: CLAUDECODE/CLAUDE_CODE for Claude Code, CODEX_SANDBOX for Codex, plus Cursor, Gemini, Pi, and the universal AI_AGENT. That single signal does two jobs: it shapes the CLI's output (more on that below) and it tags each Hub request with an agent/ user-agent, so we can attribute traffic to the agent driving it. The two largest by distinct users are Claude Code and Codex, well ahead of everything else, and they're the two agents we benchmark later in this article.

The bars count distinct users per agent; request volume is the sub-label. Claude Code alone is ~40k users and nearly 49M requests, with Codex close behind. These are early numbers (we only began attributing agent traffic in April 2026), but the scale is already significant, and we expect it to keep growing as coding agents become a standard way to work with the Hub.

Humans and coding agents expect different outputs for the same hf commands. A human wants rich terminal output: ANSI color, padded tables truncated to fit the screen, a green ✅ on success, ✔ for booleans, progress bars, prose hints. An agent wants the inverse: no ANSI, nothing truncated, every value in full since an agent can handle far denser output than a human, kept compact and structured to stay light on tokens. It also can't answer a CLI prompt and will happily re-run a command after a timeout. The rest of this section is how hf gives each side what it needs. We introduced agent-mode output in hf v1.9.0 and have been migrating the rest of the CLI to it gradually in the following releases.

When hf auto-detects agent use (via the environment variables mentioned above), it renders the same command differently. It optimizes output format for humans or agents without passing a flag:

A human gets an aligned table, truncated to fit the terminal, plus a hint on how to see more, with color cues for status (a green ✓ on success, red on error). An agent gets the complete record as TSV: full repo ids, full ISO timestamps, every tag, no ANSI codes, nothing truncated, clean to parse and light on tokens.

In practice, we've implemented logging methods like .table(...), .result(...), .json(), etc., which take raw data as input and handle the formatting. In addition to human and agent modes, we've introduced --json and --quiet options to make it easier to pipe commands together. The default mode is automatically chosen based on context, but users can always force the format of their choice with --format human | agent | json | quiet.

CLI commands rarely run in isolation: one step usually implies the next (git add, then git commit). Many hf commands now end with a hint: the exact next command to run, pre-filled with the IDs you just used, so a user or agent can chain straight to the next step instead of working it out from scratch. Start a Job in the background and it points you to its logs; create a Space and it points you to its boot status:

For a human that's a convenience. For an agent it's a rail: the next action is named, parameterized with the right ids, and ready to run, so it takes fewer steps working out what to do. Errors behave the same way, naming the fix instead of just failing:

Hints, warnings and errors all go to stderr while data goes to stdout, so none of this guidance pollutes the output the agent is parsing.

hf never sits on an interactive prompt waiting for a key an agent can't press. A destructive command still asks a human to confirm, but in agent mode it fails fast with the fix in the message (Use --yes to skip confirmation.), and -y/--yes skips it. And because agents retry on timeouts and lost context, operations are built to be safe to repeat: hf repos create --exist-ok is a no-op if the repo already exists, and re-running an upload re-commits cleanly. Separately, the commands that move real data take a --dry-run that shows exactly what they'll transfer before they run, which proves handy for humans and agents alike, since neither has to commit to a long download or blind sync:

hf is built to be probed: run hf to see the resource groups, run --help on the one you need, and every --help ends with real, copy-pasteable examples (which an agent matches against far faster than it parses a description):

The command tree is consistent, resource + verb with the obvious aliases (hf models ls, hf repos create, hf jobs ps, hf collections delete; list/ls, remove/rm), so once an agent learns one command it can guess the rest. And the output composes: -q prints one id per line to pipe into the next command, --json gives you something to hand to jq.

To find out whether the hf CLI is really more efficient for agents, we measured it. We built a small evaluation harness and ran the same set of Hub tasks through each way of driving the Hub, many times over, grading every run against the live Hub. Here's the headline before the methodology: across both agents the hf CLI comes out ahead, most clearly on complex, multi-step tasks where it uses far fewer tokens.

(self-report error = the agent reported success on the 17 solvable tasks but the Hub said otherwise. The hf CLI rows are the CLI with its skill installed; what the skill adds on top of the bare CLI (chiefly fewer tool calls) is broken out in the skill section below. Representative transcripts are published in this bucket.)

We defined 18 non-trivial Hub tasks. Not "download a file", but the kind of thing you'd actually ask for: aggregate a trending org's models, inspect a repo's files and their sizes, upload a folder with include/exclude rules, delete files, copy files across repos, open a PR that adds a license, create a repo with a branch and a tag, sync and prune a bucket, build a collection. Each task goes to a fresh coding agent with exactly one way to talk to the Hub:

We run the hf CLI in two configurations, with and without its skill (a generated command reference we come back to in its own section). But the headline comparison below is simply hf CLI vs curl / the SDK; the skill's incremental effect is small enough that we break it out on its own rather than crowd it into the main results.

The config is deliberately clean: a fresh instance per run, no custom MCP servers, no CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, nothing in context to nudge behavior. The task and the tool go into a single prompt, and the agent finishes with a TASK_COMPLETE or TASK_FAILED marker, but we don't trust that marker (an agent will report success on work that never landed), so we grade every run independently by re-querying the live Hub: did the branch really get created, is the file actually gone, does the bucket exist? Each task/tool combination is run 10 times, since coding agents are non-deterministic, about 520 runs per agent (18 tasks × 3 tools × 10 reps, minus a cap on one billable Jobs task) and ~1,000 graded runs in total. We ran the whole thing twice, on the two most popular coding agents (Claude Code with Sonnet 4.6 and OpenAI Codex with GPT-5.5).

The two charts below unpack the table above. First, task success on Sonnet, the agent where curl and the SDK struggle most:

Without the CLI, curl and the SDK trail by ten points, because on Sonnet they simply can't finish parts of the job (the writes, mostly), while the hf CLI clears them.

The second image shows token impact on GPT-5.5, broken down per task. Each bar is the curl/SDK tokens divided by the CLI's on the same task, so 2.4× means the non-hf version burned 2.4 times as many tokens to do the same thing:

On a one-shot read (count dataset rows, batch metadata) curl and the SDK are fine, and sometimes lighter. But as tasks get more complex and involve several dependent steps, the agent has to hand-roll the entire chain of REST calls (or dig through the SDK) and the cost blows up: 2.4× to 6× the CLI's on creating a repo with a branch and tag, deleting files, copying across repos, or syncing a bucket. The hf CLI lets the agent express the task as a few higher-level commands, rather than crafting a complex workflow.

hf ships a skill: a compact reference of the whole command surface that an agent loads as context. It's auto-generated from the live hf command tree, one line per command (its signature, a one-line description, and the flags that matter), grouped by resource, with a short glossary of common options. It deliberately skips the self-explanatory flags so it stays terse and light on context, and it's regenerated every release. Run hf skills preview to print it, or install it with:

What does it buy you? Mostly, the agent stops guessing. The clearest single view is how many commands each run takes, with the skill and without:

On both agents that's about ten commands per task down to about seven, roughly 30% fewer tool calls. That's because the agent isn't probing --help to find the right command and argument. The skill won't cut your token bill, because it prepends a fixed slice of info to the context, so tokens remain about the same or slightly tick up for the same task. The Skill won't make the CLI more reliable either, but it will help the agent spend time running your task rather than finding out how the tool works. This could be particularly helpful when using hf with local models.

We ran each task in a fresh session, so the skill pays its context cost on every task. In a real multi-task session that cost amortizes (the agent learns the command surface once), so the token picture likely improves there; we didn't measure that case.

We benchmarked all this because we think it matters. Agents are becoming real users of the Hub: they train models, build and clean datasets, and ship demos as Spaces, almost always on behalf of a person. A Hub that works well for agents is also a Hub that works better for the people using them. The better an agent's tools are, the more it can do for you.

If your agent interacts with the Hugging Face Hub, we recommend giving it the hf CLI:

Then hand it the skill, so it knows the whole command surface from the first turn:

Then point your agent at the Hub and let it work. Make sure you're logged in (hf auth login), then hand it a prompt like:

It'll work out the commands on its own and come back with something useful.

The full command reference lives in the hf CLI guide.

Building an agent harness? Get it registered! That's how hf learns to detect it, and how the Hub attributes its traffic to your harness. You simply need to open a small PR adding an entry to agent-harnesses.ts. Read the Register your agent harness guide for more details.

Giving AI agents access to command-line tools can make them more capable because they can interact with real development resources instead of relying entirely on generated text. The important part is setting appropriate permissions, defining task boundaries, and checking the results of commands before allowing consequential changes. I also think repeatable workflows make these integrations easier to manage, especially when the same development tasks occur frequently. This guide onhttps://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/ai-development/ai-workflow-automation-cursor-claude-commands is relevant to that idea, as reusable commands can help standardize routine coding activities. Combining tool access with clear safeguards is key to building dependable AI-assisted workflows.

#10094. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety: Customizable Multimodal Safety for Global Enterprise AI

The last two years have seen NVIDIA's content safety stack grow from a focused English text classifier into a family of specialized models—each extending coverage to new modalities, languages, and inference modes. Nemotron 3 Content Safety, released in March 2026, combined multimodal and multilingual capabilities for the first time in a single 4B-parameter model. Today, we are releasing Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety, which completes that arc: a single model that unifies multimodal input, multilingual reach, custom enterprise policy enforcement, and auditable reasoning into one inference call.

This post covers what changes in 3.5, the design decisions behind each new capability, and how to integrate the model into production safety pipelines.

Nemotron 3 introduced image understanding; Nemotron 3.5 deepens the multimodal integration. The model takes a user prompt, an optional image, and an optional assistant response as a single context window and produces a coherent safety verdict over the combined input. Evaluating all three together—rather than scoring each independently—closes a well-known gap in multimodal safety scenarios: policy violations that only emerge from the interaction between text and image, or between request and response, are now caught in a single pass.

Nemotron 3.5 maintains the 12-language explicit training coverage of its predecessors—English, French, Spanish, German, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic, Hindi, Russian, Portuguese, and Italian—while also inheriting strong zero-shot generalization across approximately 140 languages from the Gemma 3 base model. This means deployments in markets where training data is sparse (e.g., Southeast Asian languages, Scandinavian languages, less-resourced African languages) benefit from base-model multilingual transfer without requiring separate fine-tuning.

This is the most significant architectural addition in 3.5 relative to Nemotron 3. Production deployments rarely operate under a single universal safety taxonomy. A healthcare platform has a different risk profile than a financial services chatbot, a developer tools IDE, or a children's education app. Nemotron 3.5 accepts a custom policy specification alongside the input. The model reasons over that policy when producing its verdict rather than deferring entirely to the built-in taxonomy. This extends the work first introduced in Nemotron Content Safety Reasoning 4B to the full multimodal, multilingual setting.

Every safety verdict in Nemotron 3.5 can be accompanied by an auditable reasoning trace via an optional think mode. When enabled, the model outputs its step-by-step reasoning before delivering a final safe / unsafe label and, optionally, the violated categories.

When latency is the primary constraint, THINK mode can be disabled to return to the same low-latency binary verdict available in Nemotron 3.

With Nemotron 3.5, we are releasing our safety dataset. This is an important milestone since most OSS safety models don't generally provide the training or evaluation sets. This problem is worse for the multimodal space where artifacts such as images or videos are often derived from resources with restrictive licensing terms. The Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety Dataset is multimodal, multilingual, and includes safety reasoning traces that were used to train the model. These reasoning traces were generated in a 2-step manner to make them concise, similar to the Nemotron Content Safety Reasoning 4B model.

Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety is built on Google Gemma 3 4B IT (4B parameters), providing a 128K context window, strong vision-language reasoning, and broad multilingual coverage. NVIDIA fine-tunes this base with a LoRA adapter that installs targeted safety classification behavior while keeping the model compact enough for real-time deployment on 8GB+ VRAM GPUs.

The inference interface supports three output modes:

Mode 3 — THINK mode (reasoning + verdict):

The safety taxonomy follows the Aegis 2.0 framework: 13 core categories aligned with the MLCommons safety taxonomy, plus 10 fine-grained subcategories. This alignment allows direct comparison with other open and closed guard systems benchmarked on Aegis-taxonomy datasets.

Reasoning is a supercharger for content safety classification because it provides the necessary context, customization, and accountability required for production AI systems, especially in enterprise and regulated environments.

Enables Custom and Contextual Policy Enforcement

Reasoning allows a content safety model to dynamically interpret and enforce custom, domain-specific policies defined in natural language at the time of inference. This is necessary because production deployments rarely operate under a single, universal safety taxonomy. A financial services chatbot has a different risk profile than a children's education app which may have a lower tolerance for profanity. This capability supports:

Provides Auditable and Documented Justification

The reasoning traces show the model's step-by-step logic before it delivers a final safe or unsafe verdict. This documented justification serves several purposes:

While reasoning can introduce latency, the Nemotron model addresses this by condensing reasoning chains into concise summaries to limit output tokens and increase efficiency. This is done in a 2-step process similar to what was done in the predecessor model Nemotron-Content-Safety-Reasoning-4B. In the first step, we use larger, more powerful models such as Qwen 397B to generate chain-of-thought reasoning traces based upon provided prompts, images, and responses. We also provided the ground-truth labels of the samples to avoid any misclassification that can find its way into the reasoning traces. In step 2, we make these reasoning traces more concise by using another large model such as Qwen 80B. We specifically instruct this model to rephrase the original traces (from step 1) so that it fits in no more than 3 sentences. Based on our experiments, most reasoning traces generated are under 3 sentences.

The efficient reasoning traces optimization allows for low-latency custom policy enforcement. Furthermore, the reasoning traces provide a valuable training signal that can be used for training specialized moderator models. Developers can choose a dual-mode operation, disabling reasoning for minimal latency in generic tasks or enabling it for complex policies.

The dataset driving Nemotron 3.5 is an evolution of the multimodal, multilingual blends used for Nemotron 3, with additions targeting the reasoning and custom-policy capabilities. We have used the following sources of data:

Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety was evaluated across multilingual, multimodal, and custom-policy safety benchmarks, including VLGuard, MM-SafetyBench, PolyGuard, RTP-LX, Aya Redteaming, XSafety, MultiJail, Aegis, Dynaguardrail, and CoSA. These evaluations reflect the core production challenge for enterprise safety: applying consistent guardrails across global languages, text and image inputs, and domain-specific policies without adding significant latency.

Nemotron 3 set a strong baseline with 84% average accuracy on multimodal harmful-content tests and roughly half the latency of LlamaGuard-4-12B. Nemotron 3.5 maintains that compact 4B efficiency while adding custom policy support and reasoning traces.

Across multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks, Nemotron 3.5 delivers strong harmful-content classification accuracy while maintaining a compact footprint. This matters because many safety models remain English-first, text-only, or too costly to run repeatedly in production pipelines. Nemotron 3.5 is designed to combine multilingual coverage, multimodal classification, custom-policy support, and low-latency deployment in one model.

Figure 1. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety delivers strong harmful-content classification accuracy across multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks, averaging about 85% across the evaluated benchmark set.

The language-level results highlight why multilingual safety matters for global enterprise AI. On Multilingual Aegis, Nemotron 3.5 averages 96.5% harmful-content classification accuracy across 12 languages. On RTP-LX, it averages 88.8%, for a combined Aegis and RTP-LX average of 92.7%. This consistency helps teams apply the same safety posture across customer, employee, and partner-facing workflows instead of relying on English-only moderation or separate regional safety models.

Figure 2. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety averages 97% harmful-content classification accuracy on Multilingual Aegis Cultural + Adapted (prompt classification) (harmful-f1) across 12 languages.

Figure 3. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety averages 89% harmful-content classification accuracy on RTPLX (prompt classification) (harmful-f1) across 12 languages.

Accuracy alone is not enough for production guardrails. Safety models must also be efficient enough to run before content is processed, returned, or routed downstream. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety's compact 4B design helps reduce the cost and latency of repeated safety checks, making multilingual and multimodal guardrails practical for real-world AI applications.

The latency profile is unchanged from Nemotron 3 in the default (no THINK) mode. THINK mode adds inference time proportional to trace length, but this overhead is predictable and can be budgeted separately from the synchronous moderation loop—for instance, by running THINK-mode evaluation asynchronously as part of an audit pipeline while the default mode handles real-time decisions.

Figure 4. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety achieves 3x lower end-to-end latency on a multimodal benchmark compared to an alternative multimodal safety model.

Compared to another reasoning safety model, our model generated up to 50% fewer tokens when reasoning is enabled, making it efficient in terms of cost and latency.

A recurring theme in multimodal safety research is the gaps in existing evaluation infrastructure. Nemotron 3.5's development encountered the same gaps documented in the broader literature:

NVIDIA's multimodal training data—with real images and culturally nuanced multilingual prompts—is designed to fill some of these gaps for model training. The benchmark gap for evaluation remains an open problem for the broader safety research community.

Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety is available on Hugging Face under the NVIDIA Open Model License for research and commercial use, along with the training dataset. It supports transformers, vLLM, and SGLang, and is available as a production-grade NVIDIA NIM on build.nvidia.com for teams that need a pre-packaged, GPU-optimized inference microservice.

Developers can also access the model through inference platforms including Baseten, Eigen AI, DeepInfra, OpenRouter, and Vultr.

For custom policy workflows, NVIDIA provides a Claude- and Codex-compatible skill for generating custom policies, along with cookbooks showing how to use the model. Custom policies and reasoning traces help teams adapt safety behavior to domain-specific rules while keeping decisions auditable.

#10092. A Practical Guide to Browser Developer Tools for Debugging and Improving Websites

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Building a website involves more than writing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Developers also need to test how their code behaves in different browsers, identify layout problems, investigate JavaScript errors, and understand why certain pages take longer to load.

Browser developer tools make these tasks easier. They provide a way to inspect the code currently running in a browser without constantly changing files or guessing what might be wrong.

Whether you're developing a new website or maintaining an existing application, learning to use these tools can improve your debugging workflow and help you write more reliable code.

Let's explore some useful browser development tools and how to apply them to everyday web development tasks.

Browser developer tools, commonly called DevTools, are built-in utilities available in modern browsers such as Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge, and Safari.

They allow developers to examine a webpage's HTML structure, modify CSS properties, debug JavaScript, inspect network requests, and test responsive layouts.

You can usually open them by right-clicking a webpage and selecting Inspect. On Windows and Linux, the F12 key or Ctrl + Shift + I shortcut also opens DevTools in most browsers.

The following table highlights some commonly used features:

Understanding what each panel does makes it easier to select the right tool for a particular problem.

The Elements panel is one of the most frequently used features in browser DevTools.

It displays the Document Object Model (DOM), which represents the structure of the webpage currently loaded in the browser. Developers can select individual elements and examine the CSS rules affecting their appearance.

For example, imagine that a heading has more spacing than expected. Instead of immediately editing the stylesheet, inspect the heading and review its computed styles.

You might discover that the spacing comes from a margin inherited through another CSS rule or from a conflicting selector.

You can also experiment with CSS properties directly inside DevTools.

If the card appears too wide, you can temporarily change its width or padding in the Styles panel.

The browser immediately displays the result, allowing you to compare different values without repeatedly editing and saving your stylesheet.

However, these temporary changes do not automatically update your original CSS files. Once you've identified the correct solution, apply it to your project source code.

For more detailed CSS debugging techniques, developers can also read SitePoint's guide on CSS Debugging and Optimization: Browser-based Developer Tools.

JavaScript errors can prevent interactive features from working correctly. A navigation menu might stop opening, a form might fail to submit, or a button might not trigger the expected action.

The Console panel helps developers investigate these problems.

For example, consider the following JavaScript:

If the page does not contain an element with the ID submitButton, the selected value will be null. Calling addEventListener() on that value causes an error.

You can prevent this particular issue by checking whether the element exists:

The Console panel also allows developers to execute JavaScript expressions manually.

This returns the number of image elements currently present in the document.

You can use similar expressions to inspect elements, check values, and test small pieces of functionality.

Sometimes a JavaScript error is not immediately visible. A function may execute successfully but produce an unexpected result.

In such cases, the Sources panel in Chrome DevTools or the Debugger panel in Firefox can help.

A breakpoint pauses JavaScript execution at a specific line. Developers can then inspect variable values, examine the call stack, and execute the code step by step.

If the application displays an incorrect total, you can place a breakpoint inside calculateTotal().

When the function executes, the browser pauses and allows you to inspect the values of price, quantity, and total.

This is more useful than repeatedly adding console.log() statements throughout a large application.

Breakpoints are particularly helpful when debugging complex functions, asynchronous operations, and event handlers.

A webpage may contain several resources, including images, stylesheets, JavaScript files, fonts, and API requests.

If one of these resources fails to load, part of the website may stop working correctly.

The Network panel provides information about requests made by the browser.

It displays request URLs, HTTP status codes, response sizes, loading times, and other useful details.

For example, the following table explains some common HTTP responses developers may encounter:

Suppose an image is missing from a product page. Open the Network panel, reload the page, and filter the requests by images.

If the image returns a 404 response, check whether the file path is correct and whether the resource exists on the server.

The same process can help investigate failed API requests.

For example, if a frontend application requests product information from an API, the Network panel allows you to inspect the request method, response status, and returned data.

This helps developers distinguish between frontend problems and backend errors.

A website that looks correct on a desktop computer may not work properly on a smartphone.

Text can overflow, navigation menus can become difficult to use, and images may extend beyond their containers.

Browser DevTools include responsive design and device emulation features that allow developers to test different viewport sizes.

In Chrome, you can enable the device toolbar from the DevTools interface. Firefox provides a similar feature called Responsive Design Mode.

The desktop layout displays three columns, while smaller screens display one column.

You can test this behavior by changing the viewport width inside DevTools.

A useful responsive testing process includes:

Checking common mobile and tablet widths.

Testing both portrait and landscape orientations.

Checking whether navigation remains usable.

Verifying that buttons and links are easy to interact with.

Device emulation is useful during development, but it does not completely replace testing on physical devices.

A website can have correct HTML, CSS, and JavaScript but still provide a poor experience if it loads slowly or performs unnecessary work.

The Performance panel helps developers investigate browser activity over time.

It can record page interactions and provide information about scripting, rendering, painting, and other browser operations.

For example, a page might become unresponsive when a user opens a navigation menu. A performance recording can help identify whether a long-running JavaScript function is blocking the main thread.

Developers can also use tools such as Lighthouse to audit performance, accessibility, SEO, and other aspects of a webpage.

Instead of making random optimization changes, use the available measurements to identify the actual problem.

Some useful areas to investigate include:

Performance analysis should be repeated after making changes to determine whether the optimization actually improves the result.

These features are useful, but they can also introduce debugging challenges.

For example, an application might continue displaying outdated information because an old value remains stored in local storage.

The Application panel in Chrome DevTools allows developers to inspect and manage several types of browser storage.

If the application behaves unexpectedly because of stored data, inspecting local storage can help identify the problem.

Be careful when clearing storage because doing so may remove authentication sessions, saved preferences, or other application data.

Knowing individual DevTools features is useful, but developers benefit even more from using them in a consistent order.

The following workflow can make troubleshooting more efficient:

This process helps developers identify the cause of a problem before changing multiple parts of the application.

It also makes debugging easier when working with other developers because the issue can be reproduced and explained using specific observations.

Browser developer tools are essential for modern web development. They help developers inspect HTML and CSS, debug JavaScript, analyze network requests, test responsive layouts, and investigate performance issues.

The most effective approach is to select the appropriate tool for the problem instead of making changes based on assumptions.

Whether you're working on a small website or a complex web application, becoming familiar with DevTools can make your development workflow more efficient and help you build websites that are easier to maintain.

Rather than treating debugging as something that happens only after development, make it a regular part of your workflow. This allows you to identify problems earlier, verify your solutions, and deliver more reliable web experiences.

#10090. The Open Source Community is backing OpenEnv for Agentic RL

OpenEnv is a tool for creating an agentic execution environment like terminals, browsers, or anything an agent can interact with. And today, we’re excited to announce that OpenEnv is becoming even more open, to make the future of training agents open source.

Starting today, OpenEnv will be coordinated by a committee that so far includes Meta-PyTorch, Reflection, Unsloth, Modal, Prime Intellect, Nvidia, Mercor, Fleet AI, Microsoft, Hugging Face, and RadixArk. OpenEnv now lives at huggingface/OpenEnv

OpenEnv project is supported and adopted by some of the leading organizations in the AI ecosystem, including PyTorch Foundation, vLLM, SkyRL (UCB), Lightning AI, Axolotl AI, Stanford Scaling Intelligence Lab, Mithril, OpenMined, Scaler AI Labs, Scale AI, Patronus AI, Surge AI, Halluminate, Turing, Scorecard, Snorkel AI, SGLang, and Miles.

Agent harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, and Hermes just keep improving. One reason for their improvement is that models like GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 are trained to use their respective harnesses.

We want those gains with open source models too: training local models that use harnesses effectively, and saving compute by specializing models for specific tasks.

Frontier labs train models and harnesses that, for the most part, work like hand in glove. The model is trained to use the harness and optimised for its characteristics. Models can generalise beyond these harnesses, to some extent, but nothing beats the efficiency of training.

In the open, this isn’t the case. Developers use any harness, any model, any inference engine, on whatever use case they value. This is fundamental to the community, but it’s also a challenge that requires infrastructure and tooling to tackle.

That’s where OpenEnv comes in. It’s a library to interface between harness, environment, and trainer, which works on any model. For this to stick, it will need to be owned by all the major stakeholders.

Alongside the governance change, we're tightening what OpenEnv is.

In recent releases, OpenEnv has become an interoperability layer for RL environments. Its job is to standardize how environments are published, deployed, and consumed by agents. It will not dictate how rewards are defined or how training loops work. Reward definition, scoring rubrics, and trainer-specific logic belong in the libraries that specialize in them. OpenEnv is the common socket they can all plug into.

One interface, many environments which all expose the familiar Gymnasium-style API (reset(), step(), state()) running on a client/server architecture. A trainer that speaks OpenEnv can drive any compliant environment without bespoke code.

Familiar protocols and canonical packaging. Environments are served over standard protocols like HTTP and WebSocket and packaged with Docker. MCP is a first-class citizen, so OpenEnv environments are instantly compatible with MCP servers and the same environment behaves consistently in both simulation (train/eval) and production modes.

Interop across env libraries. You can define and consume environments across different ecosystems (verifiers, harbor, and others) and on the infrastructure and hub of your choice. OpenEnv is the deployment and interface layer underneath them, rather than a competitor to them.

Over the coming months we will focus on the things that turn OpenEnv from a fast-growing project into a dependable standard:

OpenEnv is community-centric by design, and it's still early — expect rough edges, and help us smooth them. Check out the code and RFCs: github.com/openenv/OpenEnv

Thanks to everyone who helped make this transition happen. Let's build the common substrate for open-source agentic RL together.

There is some excellent work here to check. https://a2eprotocol.github.io/docs/

#10086. Migrating Your GitHub CI to Hugging Face Jobs

If you have a GitHub repository and you have GitHub Actions enabled, you probably use GitHub-hosted runners for CI. That is the default for many projects because it is simple: add a workflow, write runs-on: ubuntu-latest, and GitHub gives you a machine.

That default is convenient, but it also has limits. GitHub Actions can be slow or down for maintenance, the hosted machines are generic, and GPU access is not something most open-source projects can just turn on. For Trackio, those limits started to matter. We wanted both reliable CPU CI for basic unit tests and frontend checks, but also GPU CI for tests that need to run on actual CUDA hardware.

So built an alternative: keep GitHub Actions in charge of CI, but run the jobs on Hugging Face Jobs.

The result: Trackio's CI now runs on Hugging Face Jobs and streams back real-time logs, cutting our CI time for CPU jobs by about 30% and enabling a whole new test suite that runs on GPU machines!

In this article, we explain step-by-step how to recreate the same setup for your GitHub repo. If you are using an agent, you can point it to this article, since we provide CLI instructions alongside browser-based instructions for us humans.

Let's start with a quick intro to Hugging Face Jobs!

Hugging Face Jobs lets you run commands or scripts on Hugging Face's serverless infrastructure with almost any hardware flavor. A Job is essentially:

That makes Jobs a natural fit for CI. CI jobs are already command-driven, already run in clean environments, and often benefit from choosing exactly the right hardware. For ML libraries, the GPU case is especially compelling: you can run a test suite on real GPU hardware without maintaining your own always-on runner.

The key step is connecting GitHub Actions to HF Jobs, which we describe below.

For this setup, we created huggingface/jobs-actions, a small bridge that turns a GitHub Actions job into an ephemeral self-hosted runner running inside an HF Job.

From GitHub's point of view, this is just a self-hosted runner. From Hugging Face's point of view, it is just a Job that launches a container to run the workflow steps from the repo’s GitHub Actions.

The first thing you need is the dispatcher. This is a small Docker Space that receives GitHub workflow_job webhook events and launches HF Jobs in response.

Create this first because the GitHub App needs a webhook URL, and that URL comes from the Space. This Space should be under your own namespace or under a Hugging Face org that you have write access to.

Go to huggingface/jobs-actions-dispatcher and click Duplicate this Space.

Use cpu-upgrade for real CI so the dispatcher stays available for GitHub webhooks. cpu-basic is fine for testing and will probably work, but it can sleep after inactivity; if GitHub's webhook arrives while it is waking up, the workflow may stay queued forever.

After it builds, open the duplicated Space. You will see a section that says "Required Space secrets," which you can ignore for now. The landing page should display the GitHub App webhook URL you need in the next step. It will look like this:

If you'd prefer to set up the dispatcher Space with an agent or use a CLI workflow:

Next, create and install the GitHub App from the dispatcher Space itself. This App needs permission to listen for queued workflow jobs and create ephemeral self-hosted runner registration tokens.

In the setup form, enter the GitHub repo whose CI should run on HF Jobs:

Then click the button to create the GitHub App. GitHub will ask you to choose a name for the App; the name can be anything, as long as it is available in your GitHub account or org. After you submit, the final screen tells you exactly how to upload the App credentials to the dispatcher Space with the hf CLI.

Important note: you will need to provide an Hugging Face token that has permissions to launch Jobs, corresponding to your personal account or an org under which Jobs should be charged. This token should be saved as the HF_TOKEN secret in your dispatcher Space.

Finally, you will install the App on the same GitHub repo you entered in the Space. In the Trackio setup, we installed it on gradio-app/trackio.

The GitHub App manifest flow is still browser-based, but an agent can follow the same Space-driven path:

Paste $GITHUB_REPO into the Space, click the GitHub App creation button, choose any available App name, and follow the generated GitHub instructions.

After the App exists, install it on your repo from the App settings page. For a GitHub org, the installation settings are under:

At this point, the dispatcher Space should be configured. The GitHub App setup flow generated the commands that upload the App credentials, webhook secret, and Hugging Face token to the Space.

By default, HF Jobs are launched under the same namespace as the dispatcher Space. Optionally, set HF_NAMESPACE as a Space variable if you want to bill jobs to a different Hugging Face user or org:

The token you set in Step 2 should correspond to this namespace.

The actual workflow change is small. Instead of:

use one of the labels handled by the dispatcher:

For any GitHub Action you'd like to run on HF Jobs, this 1-line change is all you need!

To add a minimal smoke-test workflow from the CLI:

You should be able to see logs just like a regular GitHub Action—for example, in this Trackio PR #565.

Our first CPU setup used ubuntu:22.04 and installed missing system packages during every run. That worked, but it was slower than it needed to be. GitHub's ubuntu-latest image includes a lot of developer tooling by default; a bare Ubuntu image does not.

For Trackio, the UI tests need Playwright browsers, Node, ffmpeg, sqlite, git, and normal Linux build dependencies. Hugging Face Jobs supports using any Docker image, so we switched to the Microsoft Playwright image, which worked well:

Here are the numbers from the Trackio CI:

The biggest win was GPU CI. The Trackio GPU check ran on HF Jobs and passed in 45s, costing less than a cent at the t4-small rate for that duration.

The CPU result was also encouraging. With the right image, the Linux test job was faster than the GitHub-hosted baseline. That suggests HF Jobs can be a practical CI backend, especially for ML projects that need custom images or accelerators.

Logs were another pleasant surprise. GitHub Actions logs are useful, but the web UI can be heavy for large logs. HF Jobs logs are easy to fetch from the CLI:

That makes them easy to inspect with local tools or coding agents. In our bridge, we also mirrored the GitHub Actions job log into the HF Job log, so either system had enough information to debug a run.

Finally, although we didn't need them for Trackio's CI, HF Jobs also supports mounting volumes, which can be very helpful if you need to load datasets or models from Hugging Face quickly as part of your CI.

Hopefully, this gives you all you need to try HF Jobs for running your GitHub Actions!

#10084. How to Add Idempotency Keys to a Node.js API with PostgreSQL

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A mobile app sends POST /orders. The server creates the order, but the response is lost when the phone switches from Wi-Fi to 4G. The app sees a timeout and retries. Now the customer has two orders, and your support team has a refund to process.

Retrying is the right thing for a client to do. The problem is that POST is not idempotent: RFC 9110 defines GET, PUT and DELETE as idempotent methods, but not POST or PATCH. Repeating a POST can repeat its side effects.

An idempotency key fixes this. The client generates a unique key for each logical operation and sends it with every attempt. The server does the work once, stores the response against the key, and returns the stored response for any retry. The IETF HTTPAPI working group is standardizing this pattern as the Idempotency-Key HTTP header field, and this tutorial follows its recommendations.

We'll build it with Node.js, Express 5 and PostgreSQL. By the end you'll have a table that stores keys, a function that safely claims a key under concurrent requests, an Express route that replays stored responses, and a client that retries without creating duplicates.

The client's job is simple: generate a key, usually a UUID, and send the same key on every retry of the same operation. The draft defines the header value as a quoted string:

The server's job is harder, because every request falls into one of five cases:

To tell case 3 from case 4, the server stores a fingerprint of the request alongside the key. A matching fingerprint means a genuine retry; a different one means key reuse. Case 5 is the one most implementations get wrong, because it only shows up under concurrency. A database constraint handles it for us.

Create a project and install the two dependencies:

The key table records who sent the key, the request fingerprint, whether the work has finished, and the response to replay:

Two details matter here. The primary key includes client_id, so keys are scoped per client: two customers who happen to generate the same value can't see each other's responses. And locked_until lets the server recover a key whose request crashed halfway, which we'll use in Step 3.

The draft defines the header value as a structured field string, which means it arrives wrapped in double quotes. Many clients send it without quotes, so the parser below accepts both and limits the characters and length it will store:

The fingerprint has to be identical for identical requests, even if a client serializes the JSON body with its properties in a different order. Sorting object keys before hashing takes care of that. The hash uses SHA-256 from Node's built-in crypto module:

Including the method and path means a key reused on a different endpoint counts as a mismatch, not as a retry.

The tempting approach is to SELECT the key, and insert it if nothing comes back. Under concurrency that fails: two retries arriving a few milliseconds apart both see no row, and both do the work.

Instead, let the primary key decide. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING either inserts the row or does nothing, atomically, even across many application processes. The PostgreSQL INSERT documentation describes this behavior in detail. If the insert returns a row, this request owns the key. If not, we read the existing row and decide which case we're in:

The UPDATE in the last step is also atomic. If two retries find the same expired lock, only one of them matches the locked_until < now() condition and gets the key. If the row disappears between the two queries, for example because it was released after a failure, the function reports in_progress and the client simply retries.

Set LOCK_SECONDS comfortably above the slowest time your operation takes. If the lock expires while the original request is still running, a retry can take over and run the work a second time.

Once a request owns the key, it creates the order and marks the key as completed. Both writes happen in one transaction, so there is no moment where the order exists but the key still says in_progress, or the other way round. Note that a transaction in node-postgres has to use a single client checked out from the pool, as the node-postgres transaction documentation explains:

releaseKey runs when the work fails. Deleting the claim lets the client retry with the same key instead of waiting for the lock to expire. It only deletes rows that are still in progress, so a completed response is never thrown away.

The route validates the body first. A request with invalid input never touches the key table, so the client can fix the input and resend with the same key. Error responses use the application/problem+json format from RFC 9457, which the idempotency draft also uses in its examples:

The server side only works if the client keeps the key stable. The most common client bug is generating a new key inside the retry loop, which turns every retry into a new operation. Generate the key once per logical action, before the first attempt:

The catch branch is the reason idempotency keys exist. After a timeout, the client can't know whether the order was created. With a stable key, retrying is safe either way: if the first attempt succeeded, the retry returns the stored order; if it didn't, the retry creates it. The random jitter spreads retries out, so many clients recovering from the same outage don't all hit the server at once.

In a browser or mobile app, store the key with the pending action, for example in the form state or a local queue. If the user taps "Place order" again after an error, reuse it. Only generate a new key when the user starts a genuinely new action.

Keys can't live forever, or the table grows without limit. The draft leaves the retention period to the server but says it should be published in the API documentation, so clients know how long a retry stays safe. Twenty-four hours covers most retry scenarios. A scheduled job can delete older rows in batches:

Run it every few minutes from cron or your job scheduler until it deletes zero rows. Deleting in batches keeps each transaction short, and the created_at index from Step 1 keeps the inner query fast. A retry that arrives after its key has expired is treated as a new request, which is why the retention period belongs in your documentation.

Start the server with node server.js, then send the same request twice:

The second request lists the properties in a different order, and it's still recognized as a retry because of the canonical fingerprint. Both responses carry the same order ID, and the orders table contains one row.

Now change the quantity while keeping the key. The server answers 422, because the key now belongs to a different request:

To see the concurrent case, add await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 3000)); before completeKey in the route, restart the server, and fire two requests with a new key at the same time:

One request prints 201 and the other 409. Without the ON CONFLICT claim, both would have printed 201 and created two orders. Remove the delay when you're done.

This design guarantees that the database work in Step 4 happens once per key. Two situations need extra care:

Idempotency keys don't replace other safeguards either. A unique constraint on a natural business key, such as one payment per invoice, still catches duplicates that arrive with different keys, for example when a user submits the same form from two tabs.

With one table, an atomic claim and a transaction that stores the response next to the work, POST endpoints become safe to retry. Clients get a simple rule: generate one key per action, reuse it on every retry. The server takes care of the rest, including the concurrent retries that a SELECT-then-INSERT approach misses.

The same pattern works for PATCH endpoints and for webhooks you send to other systems. Start with the endpoints where a duplicate costs real money or confuses a customer, and publish your key format and retention period in the API documentation so client developers know what to send.

#10082. How an Agent Built a 3D Paris Gallery by Chaining Two Hugging Face Spaces

An agent built a 3D Paris gallery from two Hugging Face Spaces.

I asked a coding agent to build a beautiful website showcasing the monuments of Paris as 3D Gaussian splats. I never opened an image generator. I never touched a 3D reconstruction tool. The agent produced every asset (the images and the 3D splats) by calling two Hugging Face Spaces directly, then wired them into a cinematic viewer.

Here's the result, live as a static Space:

This post is about how that's possible now, and why I think it's a preview of how a lot of multimedia software gets built from here on.

Mitchell Hashimoto recently described a shift he calls the building block economy: the most effective path to software is no longer a polished monolith, but small, well-documented components that others (increasingly agents) can assemble. His key observation: AI is okay at building everything from scratch, but it is really good at gluing together proven pieces.

That thesis has mostly been told with code libraries. But the same forces are hitting multimedia AI. The hard part of using a state-of-the-art image model, a video model, a TTS model, or a 3D reconstruction model was never the model. It was the integration: SDKs, weights, GPUs, input formats, polling. If each model were instead a documented, callable block, an agent could glue them together the same way it globs together npm packages.

That's exactly what Hugging Face Spaces have quietly become.

The Hub hosts thousands of state-of-the-art models (a huge share of them open-weights), and most are deployed as interactive Spaces. As of now, every Gradio Space also exposes a plain-text agents.md that tells an agent exactly how to call it:

returns everything needed in one shot: the schema URL, the call and poll templates, how to upload files, and the auth hint:

No client library. No hardcoded integration. An agent reads that, and it can drive the Space end to end. Set an HF_TOKEN and you're going. You can find these instructions on any Gradio Space via its Agents button:

The real unlock is chaining: the output of one Space becomes the input to the next. Prompt → image → 3D. That's the whole pipeline behind this gallery.

The six source images the agent generated, all isolated on black, ready for single-image 3D reconstruction:

From there the agent did the "glue" work too. It noticed TripoSplat outputs are Y-down and flipped them upright, auto-framed each monument, compressed the .ply files to .ksplat (~3× smaller, so they load fast), built a Three.js viewer with a scroll-to-switch and drag-to-rotate UI, and deployed the whole thing as a static Space. The only human inputs were taste-level: "make it zoomed out," "replace the obelisk with something better for splatting," "the transition lingers too long."

Several of those steps were the agent reacting to reality. A wide glass pyramid splats poorly. A thin obelisk is dull. A single-view reconstruction infers the back. That is exactly the "outsourced R&D, fast iteration" loop the building-block economy predicts, except the R&D was a conversation.

The real test of a building block is how cheaply you can reuse it. Once this pipeline existed, spinning up entirely new galleries cost about one sentence each. "Create a similar Space with splats for Japan," then the same for Egypt, and the agent did the rest: six monument images, six splats, compression, a viewer, and a deployed Space, per country.

Several of those steps were the agent reacting to reality. A wide glass pyramid splats poorly. A thin obelisk is dull. A single-view reconstruction infers the back. That is exactly the "outsourced R&D, fast iteration" loop the building-block economy predicts, except the R&D was a conversation.

The real test of a building block is how cheaply you can reuse it. Once this pipeline existed, spinning up entirely new galleries cost about one sentence each. "Create a similar Space with splats for Japan," then the same for Egypt, and the agent did the rest: six monument images, six splats, compression, a viewer, and a deployed Space, per country.

Same two Spaces, same agents.md, only the prompts changed. That is the building-block economy in one line: the marginal cost of a new multimedia app falls toward the cost of describing it.

Point your own agent at a Space's agents.md and let it cook:

Paste either link into your coding agent (Claude Code, etc.), set your HF_TOKEN, and ask it to build something. The full, reproducible pipeline for this gallery, the scripts that hit those two agents.md endpoints, lives in the Space repo.

The building blocks are sitting right there on the Hub. The agents already know how to glue.

#10081. Taming Typography: Building a Modern CSS Reset

CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset. text-wrap: pretty can prevent a stranded word, container query units can scale a heading to the column it occupies, and text-box can trim the half-leading built into a line box. Some of these features are experimental and browser support is uneven, so they need guardrails rather than blind inclusion.

I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.

Use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you. I’ll walk you through all the details in this article and give you the full code at the end.

font-synthesis: none stops a browser from inventing bold or italic when the family lacks that face. The smoothing and text-rendering declarations are rendering hints, mainly for WebKit; results still vary by platform.

text-size-adjust disables mobile font inflation that can make a deliberately sized layout jump on rotation. font-size-adjust: from-font uses font metrics to reduce the apparent size change while a fallback swaps for a webfont.

(As with other snippets in this article, this ⁠:root block is a partial excerpt the final stylesheet combines it with additional custom properties defined later on.)

Viewport-based fluid type does not know how wide its element is. A heading in a narrow sidebar can therefore scale as though it fills the viewport.

container-type: inline-size makes the wrapper a container query, so its children can use cqi: a unit based on the container rather than the viewport. Replacing vw in clamp() lets the same heading scale appropriately in an article column or a 300px sidebar without component-specific media queries.

line-height includes space above the cap-height and below the baseline: half-leading. It becomes obvious when text must align tightly with another element. text-box-trim removes it, while text-box-edge measures from capital-letter caps to the alphabetic baseline. This is a metrics-aware alternative to font-specific negative-margin nudges.

Selectors Level 5 proposes :heading, matching h1 to h6 and [role="heading"]. It has not landed in browsers, so keep it behind an @supports selector() check.

Default heading wrapping can leave one short final line. text-wrap: balance distributes text across its lines and works best for blocks of up to about six lines. For paragraphs, text-wrap: pretty avoids a stranded final word without balancing the whole block. Both replace JavaScript orphan fixers. Editable text needs text-wrap: stable, which prevents each new word from reshuffling the paragraph.

hyphens: auto relies on the browser’s language dictionaries, so the document needs a correct lang attribute (for example ). Without one the browser has no dictionary to use and won’t be able to hyphenate text. Even with the correct lang, the defaults can leave tiny word fragments or several hyphenated lines in a row.

hyphenate-limit-chars controls the smallest breakable word and fragments; hyphenate-limit-lines prevents a ladder effect. hyphenate-limit-zone makes breaks less frequent, while hyphenate-limit-last protects the final word. Safari needs the prefixed equivalents, so declare both sets together.

Set code, variables, and headings to hyphens: manual: a broken code word can change meaning, and a hyphenated heading usually reads as an error.

Punctuation marks don’t carry the same visual weight as letters, so a quotation mark sitting at the start of a line can look slightly indented against the text below it. hanging-punctuation lets specified punctuation sit fractionally outside the text block’s edge.

The first value handles opening punctuation, and last handles closing punctuation at the end of a block, while allow-end lets punctuation hang past the right edge rather than force-wrapping. The result is a text block whose edges read as genuinely flush.

Underlines have a related problem. Browsers apply flat, one-size-fits-all thickness and position regardless of the font’s actual weight.

text-decoration-thickness: from-font reads the thickness the font’s designer intended. text-underline-offset gives descenders room to breathe, and text-decoration-skip-ink: auto interrupts the underline wherever a descender crosses it rather than drawing straight through the letter.

Variable fonts often include an optical size axis, or opsz. It lets a typeface use thinner strokes at large display sizes and thicker, more legible strokes when set small.

font-optical-sizing: auto lets the font make that adjustment based on its actual rendered size. The @supports block covers the older font-variation-settings syntax some browsers still need, while font-variant-ligatures and font-kerning enable the font’s own ligatures and kerning pairs.

Light text on a dark background genuinely reads heavier than the same weight on a light background. Where a font ships a GRAD, or grade, axis, the dark mode block dials that perceived weight down without changing glyph shape or width the way an actual weight change would. Fonts without a GRAD axis safely ignore the setting.

Mixing a monospace font into running prose often exposes a mismatched x-height at the same declared font-size. The size-adjust keyword, set once at the @font-face level, scales that font’s rendered output specifically, leaving the actual font-size value untouched.

Numbers in a table need identical widths so they stack into a clean column on the screen. Conversely, numbers in flowing text don’t need the same treatment and should sit naturally alongside the surrounding words.

The tabular-nums and lining-nums keywords give table digits a fixed width and full cap height. oldstyle-nums and proportional-nums let digits sit alongside lowercase letters without sticking up and disrupting the sentence’s texture.

font-variant-emoji makes the choice between full-colour and monochrome emoji explicit. Without it, the browser or platform gets to choose a fallback, and the result can vary more than you expect. Apply .emoji-color or .emoji-mono to containers where you want to enforce that choice, rather than setting it globally on the body.

Quote style and character order differ by language and region. English nests single quotes inside double quotes, British English reverses that convention, and French uses guillemets with a thin space.

The quotes property declares the order for each language through :lang(). The native q element then inserts the right pair through open-quote and close-quote. The same markup can render correctly in each locale without hardcoding characters into the content.

Wrapping the rules in :where() keeps them at zero specificity, so a project can override the quote style with one plain class.

Default sub and sup styling is synthesized. The browser just shrinks the text and shifts the baseline, rather than using glyphs actually designed for that position.

font-variant-position switches to the font’s own purpose-built sub and superscript glyphs where they exist, resetting vertical-align, font-size, and line-height so they don’t fight against the real glyph’s intended size and position. Most typefaces only include proper numerals rather than letters, so check the specific font before applying this broadly.

:where() always resolves to zero specificity, which is useful for a reset. Every rule here is an opinionated default, and wrapping it in :where() lets a project override a property with a plain class.

:is() solves a different problem: repetition. The heading selector list appears several times in a typographic stylesheet, and grouping it avoids the risk of forgetting a level.

Unlike :where(), :is() carries the specificity of its most specific argument.

Here’s the complete reset, combining the stable layers. Unsupported declarations are ignored by the browser, so the stylesheet can be adopted gradually.

Much of this CSS removes work that used to leak into other parts of a build. text-wrap can take over orphan handling from JavaScript, container query units keep a component’s type scale tied to its own width, and text-box-trim avoids the negative margins once used to compensate for leading. quotes, font-variant-position, and font-optical-sizing hand several smaller details back to the language and the font instead of a collection of one-off fixes.

Browser support will continue to change, especially for text-wrap and text-box-trim. Unsupported declarations are ignored, but that only helps when the unenhanced typography is acceptable in its own right.

Some of these rules are still too new for a baseline reset. A news article, a marketing page, and an editable product interface do not ask the same things of their text; the set that belongs in yours depends on the font, the content, and the browsers you still need to support.

Andy Clarke shows you how to create designs that people recognize and remember in his brand-new e-book, Standout Designs for the Web. Order it today!

"English nests single quotes inside double quotes, British English reverses that convention,"

"English nests double quotes inside single quotes, American English reverses that convention (like it usually does),"

It’s nowhere near that cut-and-dried, and double has historically and geographically been much more popular. For some reason, UK publishing mostly switched to single for the 1900s, but they seem to be returning to double these days. Very few other countries followed them to single—Canada and Australia, for example, stuck with double.

A couple of links to start with (and you can find plenty more elsewhere): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotation_mark#In_English, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotation_marks_in_English#Quotations_and_speech

Overall, :lang(en) double-first with :lang(en-GB) single-first is a decent balance. If you had :lang(en) single-first, you’d want :lang(en-US, en-CA, en-IN, en-AU, en-NZ, …) for double-first.

A more accurate wording of the first sentence would be:

Quote style and character order differ by locale and house style.

I don’t understand the reason to use font-synthesis: none;. Isn’t synthesis just a fallback for when the author makes a mistake with the font faces or when the font file doesn’t load? Users’ fallback font-families likely have weight and style variants but probably not small-caps, maybe it at least should be allowed to be synthesized.

Instead of max-width: 65ch; being applied to p, li, dd, I’d consider applying it to p, dl, ol, ul. Limiting the width of the lists, rather than the list items, prevents longer items from “sticking out” relative to the paragraphs above and below, do to the items’ inline-start margins, padding.

The browser should automatically use French-style quotes (« ») within lang=fr; appears the British quote convention is not automatically used when lang=en-GB, at least not on my USian computer.

It might be worth noting more clearly that some of these are experimental/straight up don’t work today.

hanging-punctuation is Safari-only and doesn’t seem to support quotation marks in my testing, so the text is perhaps inaccurate on that point? Many of the hyphenation properties also only work in Safari, and require the prefixes described as “legacy” in the article.

It’s mentioned briefly in the intro that some stuff is experimental, but being more explicit in the sections about what does/doesn’t work currently would be great.

Definitely cool to explore the upcoming features, but feels a bit odd to frame it as a “reset” when it will likely change how text looks in the future in untested/unexpected ways, and includes superfluous code that won’t actually impact rendering today.

Limiting body, p, li and dd width is not the job of a reset. That’s a per-site choice and should be with other per-site css, not part of a reset block. And there’s lot’s of other very opinionated stuff as well. I’ll stick with my old friend Eric Meyer.

-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased; is contentious (ill-advised); text-rendering: optimizeLegibility; is unwarranted; font-synthesis: none; has implications the typical user may not realise or like (though avoiding the need for synthesis is definitely preferable); font-size-adjust: from-font; has problematic side-effects, trading one problem for another that is in my opinion at least as bad; text-box is not widely supported and has layout implications that mean your layout will be somewhat broken in other browsers; Given the preceding ruleset, [contenteditable="true"] { text-wrap: stable; } doesn’t work if the content is within an inner p, li, dd (which it typically will be); Hyphenation is just all-round dodgy and generally better avoided; Hanging punctuation is contentious and current implementations are really not very pleasing; Turning contextual alternatives on generally is not necessarily a good idea—there’s a reason it’s opt-in and separated from the normal set of ligatures; font-kerning: normal; is ill-advised: let the browser decide, if it decides not to do kerning, it’ll be for a good reason; font-variant-position: [sub|super]; is a terrible idea when combined with font-synthesis: none, because you can’t know what font the text will be rendered in (no, your web font is not guaranteed to work; more people than you might realise block them and/or force the use of their own chosen fonts—I for one, it makes the web so much better), and the fallback font is unlikely to support the feature; and finally, :is(h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6), p, blockquote, figcaption, li is a completely useless example of :is().

Thank you for gathering these typography rules into one tidy reset — the section on font-size-adjust stood out to me, as fallback fonts so often change the apparent size of a page while a webfont loads. I also appreciated the honest note that text-box-trim and hanging punctuation are still unevenly supported, so the guardrails matter as much as the declarations themselves. It is a genuinely useful starting point that I will try on a small project first.

A reset that handles fluid type and vertical rhythm together is the part most resets skip. Hyphens in the same file is a nice touch.

I'd test the trimmed text beside an SVG icon with the webfont blocked, especially when the label wraps.

Thank you for pulling all of this together into tidy-typography.css, Stu. The section I keep coming back to is the one on rendering and fallback sanity. I spend a lot of time previewing font pairings, and the fallback swap is exactly where most sites lose their rhythm — a display face loads, the fallback is visibly narrower or taller, and the whole layout jumps. Your point about font-size-adjust: from-font reducing that apparent size change while a webfont swaps in is the clearest explanation of that fix I have read, and pairing it with font-synthesis: none so the browser does not invent a bold or italic face the family does not actually have makes the reset feel considered rather than just defensive.

The fluid typography section was the most useful part for me in practice. Using container query units so a heading scales to the column it occupies, instead of clamp() with vw scaling it as though it were always in a full-width article, solves a real problem I hit constantly: the same heading in a 300px sidebar should not behave like the same heading in the main column. The same goes for text-wrap: pretty and text-wrap: balance replacing the JavaScript orphan fixers I used to reach for, and the hyphenation tuning with hyphenate-limit-chars and hyphenate-limit-lines — I had never thought carefully about the ladder effect of several hyphenated lines in a row until this article. I also appreciated the honest framing that text-box-trim and hanging-punctuation are still unevenly supported, so they need @supports guardrails rather than blind inclusion.

One practical habit from my own work that fits well with this reset: when I test a new pairing, I preview it at small sizes with font-optical-sizing: auto on, because a face that looks crisp at display size can turn thin and hard to read at body size, and I check the same text with the webfont blocked so I can see the fallback in isolation. For anyone who wants a quick place to try out different styles side by side while testing a pairing, I keep a handy reference at https://fontsgenerators.net/ — it is useful for seeing how a style holds up before committing it to a stylesheet like this one. I will be trying tidy-typography.css as a base on my next project and keeping the experimental declarations behind @supports, exactly as you suggest.
